[i]Finally, the day had come![/i]

[i]As King Taros soldiers marched upon the city of Lanchmeta, it was apparent to all- the province of Rusumi, colloquially known as the Shield of Mitsania, was one with the Mitsa state and crown once more. This was not met with any sort of resistance, irritation, or independentist fervor- no. The token force that had been sent were greeted as heroes and treated like royalty by the locals- especially in Lanchmeta, which had previously been a small free city that maintained a strong militia.[/i]

[i]There was no opposition, however. In fact, the Mayor herself had spent months upon making it clear that this was her end goal- so long as the plateau city of Lanchmeta would be the capital. While the historical capital of Martubo did sit upon the incredibly vital Velzebil River, it had been so completely devastated by the Obengek invasions that had defined the struggle of the Mitsas for centuries that it never truly recovered. While the citys service to the crown was appreciated, Lanchmeta had become far more relevant, populous, and incredibly economically valuable as well over the past century, with the deft and even-handed policies of Mayor Varskvlavisa Tsiklauri, who, with her intellect, knowledge, and talent for public speaking, had managed to circumvent and then transform the citys once democratic system of governance into something more unashamedly anocratic. She saw no moral superiority in the democratic system- and she saw herself as the absolute best candidate to lead, so why bother with the elections? Her opponents called her an aspiring dictator at first, but these desperate cries fell on deaf ears, as her popularity continued to rise, eventually cresting the three-quarters mark in a non-binding referendum. To be fair, she had started to style herself as something more than a mere civil servant- dressing herself in more luxurious clothes, and having a wooden staff with an ornate silver cross mounted on its top end fashioned for her as a symbol of power. Still, she remained an even-handed and mostly fair ruler even after such consolidation and posturing had been done.[/i]

[i]Of course, her 17-year reign had not merely been one of consolidation. No- that popularity had to come from somewhere, and she hadnt simply deceived three quarters of the nearly 8 million people that lived in the city into liking her and accepting her rule. In fact, that was far from the truth- she had been and still was an excellent administrator, especially in terms of her well-demonstrated ability to realize Lanchmetas great economic potential, driving even more people to flock to the city. Getting the massive but untapped reserves of copper, silver, and other valuable metals out of the ground was not easy- the main challenge was sourcing the equipment, considering she was administering a landlocked city and its surroundings. She had resolved this by collaborating with the resurgent Mitsa state, which actually had ports, as well as some of the other smaller statelets along the river. This fed her popularity, which fed her ego, which fed her ambition, which led to further efforts to develop the mining sector, which led to an expansion of the citys municipality, which led to even more economic success, and the cycle renewed itself.[/i] 

[i]But she could only do so much with a mere city-state, no matter how big it got. No. She wanted more. And so she found herself becoming rather amicable to her growing economic ties with Mitsania, and considering both her and her people were ethnically Mitsa work towards integration had begun. She had begun highlighting how ties with the Mitsa state had benefited the mining sector, and the city as a whole- and she confidently asserted that full integration as a provincial capital would only further these benefits. Call it propaganda, call it an information campaign, call it whatever you want- it worked very well in quieting any whispers of opposition to the idea.[/i]

[i]And so with the lack of resistance established, she had come to personally greet the commander of the battalion-strength force that had been sent to secure Rusumis borders- with the express intent of full annexation. She was dressed well, as always, in a black silk skirt that had been modified to have a mounting point for a scabbard of sorts on the hip- which contained her iconic staff, as well as an intricate blouse that was the same shade of red as most of the Mitsa flag- with intricate embroidered details. Since it was winter, such a greeting would have to happen indoors- it was too cold outside for her delicate manner of dressing.[/i]

[i]The aforementioned commander was Major Chalkhi Koshkis, a rather standard career officer, although he did have his own personal doubts about if the ambitious mayor could be trusted. Still, he would have to play nice. Mayor Varska, as she was often colloquially referred to as, had gone out of her way to host him (although he had to halt his forces for the night to accept this!), and resultantly, he had resolved himself to avoid directly challenging her. When he arrived to the city hall, he couldnt help but notice how built-up it was, how well the expansions of the building had been integrated into the original structure- to the point that it even had a courtyard now. While he couldnt help but marvel at it, it also reminded him of the undertones of decadence that accentuated the mayors golden age of the city- he considered these tendencies dangerous. She couldnt be trusted, certainly not yet- at least, in his eyes.[/i]

[i]As he entered, he found himself impressed with how well-kept the place was- and a bit relieved to not see everything made out of gold, or some hyper-ornate show of wealth. Sure, there were subtle accents, but it wasnt overarching. He sighed, beginning to have doubts about his opinions on the rising star of Lanchmeta that was Varskvlavisa Tsiklauri. But he steeled himself from straying from his principles- no, he had to at least meet her first. At the very, very least. Then and only then would he allow himself to be even somewhat convinced of her supposed good intentions. And then the sound of someone descending the grand staircase down the hall could be heard, and without much thought, he approached. Sure enough, it was her- her staff on her hip, and her elegant and careful manner of moving and carrying herself made that clear. Of course, there was still a question to be asked- as a formality, at this point.[/i] Mayor Tsiklauri, I presume? [i]In response, she smiled, bowing slightly as a sign of respect. The expression on her face was hard to read. Was she genuinely pleased to see him? Was she merely being obsequious in the presence of the crowns forces? Or was it something else? Hell, he even doubted his doubt- was it reasonable to question everything in this way, or was he just being paranoid? Those were great questions, but they were hard to find definitive answers to. And of course, his rapid-fire thinking would be interrupted by reality.[/i] Yes. Its wonderful to have you here. I had feared that this would be overly formal and dreary. Todays a wonderful day, and we should do nothing less than celebrate it. Tomorrow, well begin in earnest, wont we? [i]This intrigued Koshkis, frankly. She was genuinely just interested in hosting him and his men to celebrate things? Huh. How odd. Maybe he [b]was[/b] being cynical about her intentions after all. Or she could just be a good liar. He had to keep his guard up, and wait before truly believing that he understood her- and more importantly, her ambitions.[/i] perhaps. My men have more ground to cover to fully secure the province. [i]She frowned slightly at this.[/i] What do you need an army for? I think Ive done a rather good job at keeping any hypothetical dissent from springing up. Dont you agree? [i]At this, Koshkis had to relent- nodding to signal that he was doing so. It was true, and he wasnt interested in being more stubborn than what was healthy.[/i] Yes, but- But what? [i]She seemed more insistent, even with just two words.[/i] But nothing, my honored guest. Come. Lets discuss tomorrows festivities. Im sure your men would appreciate a day off after all of that marching and driving. And trust me, theres [i]plenty[/i] of things to go around in this city we have more than enough to spare. So I dont want to hear it! Stay put, and let my militias handle any upstarts to our east, okay? Mission accomplished! [i]He sighed heavily. Urgh, she seemed genuinely kind, but he couldnt shake the feeling that there was something more at play! Still his superiors would be very, very upset with him if he offended her- and she seemed insistent on this celebration of hers, which she had probably spent a lot of time preparing.[/i] [b]Fine.[/b] But only one day. And you neednt send your militias in advance- just ah keep an eye on the east, so to speak. Id imagine you have contacts in the area, yes? [i]She grinned in response to his semi-begrudging acceptance of her offer.[/i] I knew youd come around. Anyone worth their reputation would do so too. Were all people, after all. [i]She paused, considering her next words.[/i] And if thats what you want, then so be it. I do have plenty of contacts, trading partners, and other quasi-associates in the eastern part of the region, which extends beyond the mostly historical borders the crown seems to be after. [i]Im sure that will be resolved with time, yes?[/i] [i]Her smile became sickly sweet towards the end of her little rambling session. It was confirmation that she was not wholly innocent or selfless, although most people werent. Still, the sense of entitlement wasnt Koshkiss favorite thing to be directly faced with.[/i] Right perhaps. In any case, your cooperation is appreciated. We couldnt set this second era of restoration in motion without your help. The mayor nodded, no longer having her face morphed into a passive-aggressive expression. It is perhaps its more than the least I could do in exchange for the economic cooperation, but it it helps everyone, yeah? 

[i]Koshkis blinked. [b]Yeah?[/b] What did she think they were, friends? He didnt [b]hate[/b] her, but they were not on casual terms. Unfortunately, he would have to suck it up for now- keeping her chuffed would keep his superiors pleased with him.[/i] I suppose it does. Its still appreciated, though. [i]She smiled once more at this, although she did suspect that he was forcing himself to tolerate her occasional bits of casuality. It didnt really matter to her, though- if she was allowed to herself without any complaints, she was fine with it.[/i] Well, thats great to hear. Now come with me and do tell me what you think your men might appreciate. Ive prepared several options for tomorrow. [i]She gestured for him to follow her upstairs, and he got the feeling that this wasnt optional if he wanted her to leave a positive review about him, so to speak. With that in mind, he obliged, and she took him to her top-floor office for a surprisingly casual discussion.[/i]

[i]The aforementioned discussion was not particularly of note- there was more of the usual cycle of Koshkis going from thinking the mayor was not so bad, to being concerned about her ambition, and then being mildly offended by her occasional lack of formality. She was an interesting person- and one he couldnt directly say no to at the moment. After the night passed, with him having to agree to allow his men to partake in the mayors planned festivities, there was a wonderful day of celebration. Even Koshkis couldnt deny that he had enjoyed himself- but on the next day, he did eventually leave the city, even if he found himself hesitant to do so. Despite his initial reservations, he had enjoyed the hospitality that the benevolent pseudo-dictator had provided him with- and the morale boost meant that on the next day, the job was done. In tandem with Tsiklauris militias, as well as plenty of local support, the entire historical province of Rusumi had been secured- as well as some more northern borderlands. Upon the official annexation of all of this land, a debate broke out immediately- should the highly popular and influential Tsiklauri be put in charge of the province as a Proveli? The title of Proveli was once one of nobility- however, in the modern day, it was merely someone appointed for life by the crown to govern a province- of which modern Mitsania only had 3 before this massive gain of territory, so the title would be a massive boost to Tsiklauris power- which some thought would sate her ambition- while others thought it would place her in a position to challenge the power of the crown- or at least that it would fuel an ambition to attain such a position. Eventually, the former opinion would win out amongst King Taros advisors- and Varskvlavisa Tsiklauri would receive the title- and the authority that came with it. Furthermore, despite some advisors begging the King to not allow this, she was able to keep her role as Mayor of Lanchmeta on top of her new position.[/i]

[i]This would please her greatly, but there was one point of low-intensity contention- the northern frontier, where Rusumis historic borders did not extend to- but Tsiklauris influence did. She wanted it to be a part of the refounded Rusumi- and most of the roughly 1 million people living in the area agreed, but such an idea was shot down- and then slated to be re-discussed at another time. This didnt agitate Tsiklauri too much, considering her ambition had been sated by her new title, but would it be enough for her forever? This question would echo in many minds, including hers- considering that her influence extended beyond present-day Rusumis borders, and she had been allowed to keep most of her militias as the Rusumi Branch of the Mitsa National Guard[/i]
